lesson.menu_desc: Defending a proposal when the room is not convinced -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 5 -- Making the Case
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando da Cunha | Lesson 5 -- Making the Case

listenings.text: I lost that room in about four minutes and it took me a year to understand how. I opened with the solution. I had the whole thing on one slide, the cost, the timeline, the return, and I was proud of how clean it was. What I had not done was spend a single sentence on the problem. So everybody in that room heard a man asking for money for something they had not yet agreed was broken. The chair let me finish and then asked, quite reasonably, what happens if we do nothing, and I did not have an answer ready, because in my head that question had been settled months earlier. It had been settled for me, not for them. The version that got approved eighteen months later was the same plan with the same numbers. The difference was that it started with two minutes on what the current line costs us every quarter, and by the time I said what I wanted, three of them had already got there on their own.

I sit through a great many of these and the thing that separates them is not the quality of the plan. It is whether the person presenting has told me the downside before I find it. When somebody names their own weakest number, unprompted, everything else they have said becomes more credible, because I now know they are not managing me. When they do not, I spend the rest of the meeting hunting, and even if I find nothing I leave less convinced than I arrived. The second thing is caveats. A number with a condition attached is stronger than a number without one, which sounds backwards until you have seen a few forecasts fall over. And the third, which almost nobody does, is ruling things out loud. If you tell me the three options you considered and rejected, and why, I do not have to wonder whether you considered them. That is thirty seconds of your presentation buying you the whole rest of it.

Roughly two thirds of pilot projects in manufacturing are judged a success by the people who ran them, and a much smaller share ever reach a full rollout. The gap is not usually about the technology, and it is rarely about money. What a pilot has that a rollout does not is attention. The best people are on it, the problems get escalated the same afternoon, and everybody involved knows they are being watched. Scale that across nine sites and the attention is the first thing you lose. Researchers who follow these programmes make a fairly unpopular recommendation. Run the pilot badly on purpose. Give it ordinary people, ordinary hours and no special access, because what you want to measure is not whether the idea can work but whether it survives a normal Tuesday. The companies that do this tend to report worse pilots and considerably better rollouts, which is an uncomfortable trade for anybody who has to present the pilot results.
